<header class="dg-head dg-head-chapter"><p class="dg-kicker">Appendix A</p><h1 class="dg-title">Computational ressources</h1></header>
<p>Almost all the figures, examples, and visualizations in these notes have been produced with <code class="dg-code">Differential Geometry Tools</code>, a Python package developed by the author alongside the text. The package is openly available at</p>
<div class="dg-center"><p><a href="https://github.com/daniellopezcano/differential_geometry"><code class="dg-code">github.com/daniellopezcano/differential_geometry</code></a></p></div>
<p>so that every figure can be regenerated, every example rerun, and every construction modified and explored by the reader.</p>
<div class="dg-skip dg-medskip"></div>
<p><strong>Open science.</strong> The repository is released under the MIT license, which allows anyone to use, modify, and redistribute the code, for teaching, research, or any other purpose, with the only requirement of preserving the original copyright and license notice. This choice reflects a conviction that runs through the whole project: educational material, like scientific results, gains value when it is transparent and reproducible. Making the code public means that the figures in these notes are not illustrations to be taken on trust, but the output of computations that anyone can inspect, check, and improve. Suggestions, corrections, and contributions are warmly welcome.</p>
<div class="dg-skip dg-medskip"></div>
<p><strong>Design goals.</strong> The package aims at providing a collection of simple, easy-to-use classes that mirror the objects introduced throughout the lectures, from manifolds, charts, and curves to fields and the structures built on top of them. Each class is kept as close as possible to its mathematical definition, so that the code can be read side by side with the text rather than as a black box. The package is built on <code class="dg-code">JAX</code>, whose automatic differentiation computes the derivatives that pervade differential geometry (Jacobians, tangent vectors, directional derivatives, or the change of components between charts) exactly and without any manual derivation. Beyond producing the figures of these notes, the same tools can be used to build more elaborate or interactive visualizations, and to test the abstract constructions on examples of one’s own choosing.</p>
<div class="dg-skip dg-medskip"></div>
<p><strong>Why code matters.</strong> Differential geometry is a subject where the formalism can easily run ahead of intuition. Writing code is a remarkably effective way of closing that gap, for at least three reasons. First, a computer accepts no vague definitions: to implement a tangent vector, a covector, or a field, one must state precisely where it lives, what it acts on, and what it returns – exactly the discipline these notes try to cultivate when specifying every map through its domain and target. Second, the distinctions that are most often blurred on paper, such as the one between a geometric object and its components in a given chart, become unavoidable in code, where every component must be computed with respect to an explicitly chosen chart. Third, abstract statements become checkable: a transformation law, the chart independence of a pairing, or the smoothness of a transition map can be verified numerically in a few lines, and one can vary a chart, a curve, or a field and immediately <em>see</em> what changes and what does not. In this sense, the package is meant as a computational counterpart to the text: not a replacement for the formal definitions, but a laboratory in which to experiment with them.</p>
<div class="dg-skip dg-medskip"></div>
<p><strong>An evolving resource.</strong> The repository is actively developed, and its contents may grow beyond what is described or used in these notes. The notes present the ideas; the repository reflects the current state of the tools built around them. Readers are encouraged to explore it, adapt it to their own needs, and use it as a starting point for visualizations and experiments of their own.</p>
